title: The Locked Room
subtitle: Staying willingly vs. being free to leave
learning_objective: Tell apart doing something voluntarily (I want to stay) from being at liberty (I could leave if I wanted) — Locke’s distinction — and connect it to Berlin’s negative and positive liberty.
disclaimer: A teaching version of Locke’s example; it illustrates his distinction and does not settle the free-will debate.

steps.title: Observe
steps.prompt: A man is carried, asleep, into a room. The door is locked. He wakes up, finds good company, and is glad to stay.

steps.title: Judge
steps.prompt: He stays because he wants to. Is he free?

steps.title: Experiment
steps.prompt: Change the conditions. Watch the two gauges: ‘does what he wants’ and ‘could do otherwise’.

steps.title: Judge again
steps.prompt: Is the man in the locked room — who wants to stay — free?
options: No, he is not free to leave

steps.title: Explain
steps.prompt: Three ways to describe what you saw.

steps.title: Apply
steps.prompt: Find the same distinction in your own life.

steps.title: Keep
steps.prompt: Keep what you understood and what you still wonder about.

user_actions.label: He knows / doesn’t know about the lock

feedback_rules.say: He does exactly what he wants — but notice the lock he doesn’t know about.
You say he is free: he does what he wants. Keep that — next, change the conditions.
You say he isn’t free, even though he is doing what he wants. What exactly is missing? Let’s look.
‘Partly’ is a good instinct — the next step separates two things that both get called freedom.
Locked and wanting to stay: he acts voluntarily, but he could not leave if he wanted to.
Now he wants to leave and can’t. The lock was there all along — wanting to leave only made it visible.
Unlocked and staying: he does what he wants and could do otherwise. Both gauges are full.
Unlocked and wanting to leave: he walks out. Doing what he wants and being able to are the same here.
Knowing about the lock changes what he feels, not whether he could leave.
You changed your mind: staying voluntarily turned out to be different from being free to leave.
This is Locke’s answer: he stays voluntarily, but he is not at liberty to leave.
You still call him free. Many people do — in the sense that he acts on his own wishes. The next step names that sense and the other one.
‘Partly’ fits: he is free in one sense and not in another.

layers.title: ① Locke: voluntary ≠ free
layers.body: Locke used this kind of case to separate two things. Staying is voluntary — he prefers it. But liberty, for Locke, is the power to act or not act as one chooses; since he could not leave if he chose to, he is not at liberty to leave.
layers.source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), Book II, ch. xxi (the locked-room example) — check the section against your edition
layers.maps_to: The lock gauge vs. the wish gauge

layers.title: ② Berlin: two concepts of liberty
layers.body: Isaiah Berlin distinguished negative liberty — how far others leave me unobstructed (the lock) — from positive liberty — being my own master, acting from my own reasons (the wish). The room shows them coming apart.
layers.maps_to: Locked door = negative liberty · own wish = positive liberty

layers.title: ③ What the room leaves open
layers.body: The room is about acting freely. Whether his wish itself is free — whether anything he wants is ultimately up to him — is the separate free-will debate (determinism, compatibilism, libertarianism). The experiment does not answer it.
layers.source: See: free will and determinism (e.g. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Free Will”)

content.map_note: The room separates two senses of freedom; it is a thinking tool, not evidence for any one theory of freedom.
